edits.location: Colour > How the setting metal changes what you see, both paragraphs
edits.issue: Unsourced factual claim ('Metal reflects into a diamond'; a warm stone looking whiter in white metal), and it is arguably the wrong way round. Convert to advice with no claim.
edits.old:
Metal reflects into a diamond. As general advice, a slightly warm stone can look whiter in white metal, while yellow or rose gold tends to blend with that warmth.

The practical step is simple: ask to see a shortlisted stone held against the metal you plan to use, in daylight as well as under shop lighting.
edits.new: The setting metal sits right against the stone, so judge colour with it in view rather than on a white tray alone. Ask to see a shortlisted stone held against the metal you plan to use, in daylight as well as under shop lighting.
edits.fix: The setting metal sits right against the stone, so judge colour with it in view rather than on a white tray alone. Ask to see a shortlisted stone held against the metal you plan to use, in daylight as well as under shop lighting.

edits.location: Shapes > Bow-tie in ovals, pears and marquise, paragraph 1
edits.issue: [[VERIFY]] 1 of 9 (fact_19, unsourced). Not essential as a claim: reword as what to look for, and drop the unsourced 'a faint shadow that moves is normal'.
edits.old: Many jewellers describe a darker, bow-tie shaped area across the middle of some elongated stones [[VERIFY: GIA or other authoritative source for the bow-tie effect in elongated shapes (fact_19)]]. As general advice, look at any oval, pear or marquise face up and turn it slowly. A faint shadow that moves is normal; a dark band that stays put through every angle is worth weighing against the stone's other qualities.
edits.new: With any oval, pear or marquise, look across the middle of the stone for a darker band, which the trade calls a bow-tie. View it face up and turn it slowly, and ask the jeweller to show you the same shape beside it for comparison. If a dark band stays put at every angle, weigh it against the stone's other qualities.

edits.old:
### Step cuts (emerald, Asscher) show clarity

Emerald and Asscher cuts use long, open, step-like facets rather than a brilliant's many small ones [[VERIFY: GIA or other authoritative source that step cuts show inclusions more readily (fact_19)]]. As general advice, treat clarity with more care in a step cut than you would in a round, and view the stone unmagnified before you settle on a grade.
edits.new:
### Step cuts (emerald, Asscher): check clarity in person

Emerald and Asscher are step cuts, with long, open facets rather than a brilliant's many small ones. Before you settle on a clarity grade for one, ask the jeweller where its inclusions are plotted, then view the stone face up without magnification.
